states.desc: A SIMULATED histogram of 1,000 one-sided p-values: 800 true nulls, uniform on (0, 1), and 200 effects of mean 3, which pile up near zero. states.readout: Universe 2001 (a median draw), 0 poor strategies: Reality Check p = 0.030; SPA-style p = 0.015, with 0 of 10 strategies recentred at their own means.
states.desc: SIMULATED universe of ten strategies, one with a true edge, plus 0 poor strategies. Each test reads its own observed statistic against its own null: the Reality Check's maximum √T·d̄ is 2.68, and the SPA-style maximum, studentized by each strategy's standard deviation, is 2.85. With no poor strategies the Reality Check's p-value is 0.030 and the SPA-style p-value 0.015; they differ because the SPA-style statistic is studentized. Adding poor strategies tends to raise the Reality Check's p-value, because each is recentred at zero and competes for the maximum.
states.title: Null distributions of the Reality Check and the SPA-style test as poor strategies are added
states.caption:
SIMULATED Each poor strategy added to the universe is recentred at zero by the Reality Check, competes for the bootstrap maximum, and pushes the null distribution to the right. The SPA-style recentring keeps poor strategies whose means fall below its threshold at those means, so its null distribution barely moves; a poor strategy that escapes the threshold can still nudge it, and the readout says how many were recentred. Each test reads its own observed statistic: the SPA-style one is studentized by each strategy's standard deviation, one reason the two p-values can differ even with no poor strategies. With no poor strategies the default is a median universe.
          Computed live in your browser on Lab 3's design at a smaller scale: 500 periods and 1,000 stationary-bootstrap resamples (mean block length 10), against Lab 3's 1,000 and 2,000, so its p-values differ from Lab 3's.

states.title: Stationary-bootstrap standard error of the mean against the block length
states.caption:
SIMULATED With positive autocorrelation (ϕ>0\phi > 0ϕ>0), short blocks miss it and understate the standard error. As blocks lengthen toward the sample size, the resample approaches a rotation of the sample and the bootstrap variance usually falls; it reaches zero only in the limit of one block. The useful block lengths lie in between, and their range depends on ϕ\phiϕ. At ϕ=0\phi = 0ϕ=0 short blocks are right on average; in a single sample, noise in the sample autocovariances can lift the curve above 1 before the long-block collapse. At ϕ=0.5\phi = 0.5ϕ=0.5 the default is a typical sample: each number in the readout lies between the 41st and 59th percentiles over 200 samples.

states.readout: Universe 2001 (a median draw), 0 poor strategies: Reality Check p = 0.030; SPA-style p = 0.015, with 0 of 10 strategies recentred at their own means.
states.desc: SIMULATED universe of ten strategies, one with a true edge, plus 0 poor strategies. Each test reads its own observed statistic against its own null: the Reality Check's maximum √T·d̄ is 2.68, and the SPA-style maximum, studentized by each strategy's standard deviation, is 2.85. With no poor strategies the Reality Check's p-value is 0.030 and the SPA-style p-value 0.015; they differ because the SPA-style statistic is studentized. Adding poor strategies tends to raise the Reality Check's p-value, because each is recentred at zero and competes for the maximum.
states.title: Null distributions of the Reality Check and the SPA-style test as poor strategies are added
states.caption:
SIMULATED Each poor strategy added to the universe is recentred at zero by the Reality Check, competes for the bootstrap maximum, and pushes the null distribution to the right. The SPA-style recentring keeps poor strategies whose means fall below its threshold at those means, so its null distribution barely moves; a poor strategy that escapes the threshold can still nudge it, and the readout says how many were recentred. Each test reads its own observed statistic: the SPA-style one is studentized by each strategy's standard deviation, one reason the two p-values can differ even with no poor strategies. With no poor strategies the default is a median universe.
          Computed live in your browser on Lab 3's design at a smaller scale: 500 periods and 1,000 stationary-bootstrap resamples (mean block length 10), against Lab 3's 1,000 and 2,000, so its p-values differ from Lab 3's.

states.title: Stationary-bootstrap standard error of the mean against the block length
states.caption:
SIMULATED With positive autocorrelation (ϕ>0\phi > 0ϕ>0), short blocks miss it and understate the standard error. As blocks lengthen toward the sample size, the resample approaches a rotation of the sample and the bootstrap variance usually falls; it reaches zero only in the limit of one block. The useful block lengths lie in between, and their range depends on ϕ\phiϕ. At ϕ=0\phi = 0ϕ=0 short blocks are right on average; in a single sample, noise in the sample autocovariances can lift the curve above 1 before the long-block collapse. At ϕ=0.5\phi = 0.5ϕ=0.5 the default is a typical sample: each number in the readout lies between the 41st and 59th percentiles over 200 samples.

states.readout: Universe 2001 (a median draw), 0 poor strategies: Reality Check p = 0.030; SPA-style p = 0.015, with 0 of 10 strategies recentred at their own means.
states.desc: SIMULATED universe of ten strategies, one with a true edge, plus 0 poor strategies. Each test reads its own observed statistic against its own null: the Reality Check's maximum √T·d̄ is 2.68, and the SPA-style maximum, studentized by each strategy's standard deviation, is 2.85. With no poor strategies the Reality Check's p-value is 0.030 and the SPA-style p-value 0.015; they differ because the SPA-style statistic is studentized. Adding poor strategies tends to raise the Reality Check's p-value, because each is recentred at zero and competes for the maximum.
states.title: Null distributions of the Reality Check and the SPA-style test as poor strategies are added
states.caption:
SIMULATED Each poor strategy added to the universe is recentred at zero by the Reality Check, competes for the bootstrap maximum, and pushes the null distribution to the right. The SPA-style recentring keeps poor strategies whose means fall below its threshold at those means, so its null distribution barely moves; a poor strategy that escapes the threshold can still nudge it, and the readout says how many were recentred. Each test reads its own observed statistic: the SPA-style one is studentized by each strategy's standard deviation, one reason the two p-values can differ even with no poor strategies. With no poor strategies the default is a median universe.
          Computed live in your browser on Lab 3's design at a smaller scale: 500 periods and 1,000 stationary-bootstrap resamples (mean block length 10), against Lab 3's 1,000 and 2,000, so its p-values differ from Lab 3's.

states.title: Stationary-bootstrap standard error of the mean against the block length
states.caption:
SIMULATED With positive autocorrelation (ϕ>0\phi > 0ϕ>0), short blocks miss it and understate the standard error. As blocks lengthen toward the sample size, the resample approaches a rotation of the sample and the bootstrap variance usually falls; it reaches zero only in the limit of one block. The useful block lengths lie in between, and their range depends on ϕ\phiϕ. At ϕ=0\phi = 0ϕ=0 short blocks are right on average; in a single sample, noise in the sample autocovariances can lift the curve above 1 before the long-block collapse. At ϕ=0.5\phi = 0.5ϕ=0.5 the default is a typical sample: each number in the readout lies between the 41st and 59th percentiles over 200 samples.
          Computed live in your browser: formula (2) evaluated exactly on one AR(1) sample of 500 observations; no Monte Carlo error.

states.readout: Universe 2001 (a median draw), 0 poor strategies: Reality Check p = 0.030; SPA-style p = 0.015, with 0 of 10 strategies recentred at their own means.
states.desc: SIMULATED universe of ten strategies, one with a true edge, plus 0 poor strategies. Each test reads its own observed statistic against its own null: the Reality Check's maximum √T·d̄ is 2.68, and the SPA-style maximum, studentized by each strategy's standard deviation, is 2.85. With no poor strategies the Reality Check's p-value is 0.030 and the SPA-style p-value 0.015; they differ because the SPA-style statistic is studentized. Adding poor strategies tends to raise the Reality Check's p-value, because each is recentred at zero and competes for the maximum.
states.title: Null distributions of the Reality Check and the SPA-style test as poor strategies are added
states.caption:
SIMULATED Each poor strategy added to the universe is recentred at zero by the Reality Check, competes for the bootstrap maximum, and pushes the null distribution to the right. The SPA-style recentring keeps poor strategies whose means fall below its threshold at those means, so its null distribution barely moves; a poor strategy that escapes the threshold can still nudge it, and the readout says how many were recentred. Each test reads its own observed statistic: the SPA-style one is studentized by each strategy's standard deviation, one reason the two p-values can differ even with no poor strategies. With no poor strategies the default is a median universe.
          Computed live in your browser on Lab 3's design at a smaller scale: 500 periods and 1,000 stationary-bootstrap resamples (mean block length 10), against Lab 3's 1,000 and 2,000, so its p-values differ from Lab 3's.
